did.abstract: The papers consist of correspondence; diaries; writings; childhood, school and college materials; financial, legal, and housekeeping records; reports; memoranda; drawings; maps; publications; artifacts; and memorabilia documenting the life and interests of Charles Augustus Lindbergh. The papers form the largest and most extensive collection of his personal, professional, and family papers. They document his work as a pilot, developer of commercial aviation and rocketry, bio-engineer, air force officer and consultant, pioneer environmentalist, Pulitzer Prize-winning author, and public figure. The papers also document his personal life, including his marriage to Anne Morrow Lindbergh, the loss of his son, and his interest in his family history. Notable correspondents include: William Benton, Kingman Brewster, Richard E. Byrd, Alexis Carrel, William E. Castle, Michael Collins, James H. Doolittle, W. L. Glenn, Robert Goddard, Harry Guggenheim, Donald A. Hall, Herbert Hoover, Thomas Lamont, James Newton, Harold Nicolson, Edward Rickenbacker, S. Dillon Ripley, Franklin D. Roosevelt, Igor Sikorsky, Lowell Thomas, Russell Train, Juan Trippe, Billy Wilder, Robert E. Wood, and Orville Wright. Notable family correspondents include his wife, Anne Morrow Lindbergh, and his mother, Evangeline Lodge Land Lindbergh. The family papers include those of Evangeline Lodge Land Lindbergh, a teacher; his father Charles August Lindbergh; and his grandfather Charles Henry Land, a pioneer dentist and inventor of the porcelain crown.

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Charles Augustus Lindbergh (1902 Feb 4-1974 Aug 26), aviator, author, biologist, and engineer, was the son of Charles August Lindbergh, a lawyer and congressman, and Evangeline Lodge Land, a science teacher whose father was Dr. Charles Land, a dentist and inventor. Born in Detroit, Lindbergh grew up in Little Falls, Minnesota, and Washington, DC. After studying engineering at the University of Wisconsin for three semesters, he left in1922 to become an airplane pilot and barnstormer. In 1925 he graduated first in his class from the United States Army Air Service Flying School and became chief pilot of the new airmail line from St. Louis to Chicago.

On May 21, 1927, Lindbergh completed the first non-stop transatlantic flight from New York to Paris and was awarded the first Distinguished Flying Cross and the Congressional Medal of Honor. This feat, followed by the publication of his best-selling book We , great public receptions in Washington and New York, and an air tour making eighty-two stops in forty-eight states followed by one to Latin America in 1927 to 1928 revolutionized commercial air service. Lindbergh worked with Juan Trippe, Henry Ford, Amelia Earhart, Will Rogers and others to develop a number of airlines, including Pan American Airways and TWA. After his marriage to Anne Spencer Morrow in 1929, the internationally famous couple conducted scientific air explorations that led to the first transoceanic air passenger service. He and Anne had six children: Charles, Jr.; Jon; Land; Scott; Anne; and Reeve, between 1932 and 1945. The tragic kidnapping and murder of their son Charles, Jr., in 1932 was called "The Crime of the Century."

In the 1930s Lindbergh became a biomedical engineer with Dr. Alexis Carrel at the Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research (now Rockefeller University) and invented the perfusion pump, a prototype of the artificial heart, documented in their book, The Culture of Organs . To protect their son Jon from unwelcome press attention, the Lindberghs moved to England in 1935 and in 1938 to France to live near Carrel. At the request of the American Embassy in Germany, Lindbergh made five trips from 1936 to 1938 to evaluate German air power for the U.S. State Department. The Lindbergh family returned to the United States in 1939. Before and after World War II, he served in the United States Air Force, but resigned to speak out against American intervention and joined the America First Committee in 1941. During the war Lindbergh served as technical consultant for the Ford Motor Company developing the B-24 bomber and for United Aircraft testing fighter planes. He also conducted air altitude flying tests at the Mayo Clinic Aero Medical Unit using himself as a guinea pig and invented the "jump bottle," to provide oxygen to flyers when they lost consciousness. As a civilian advisor he flew fifty combat missions in the South Pacific in 1944.

After the war Lindbergh served on numerous government advisory committees concerned with aviation training, national security, and space exploration. In 1954 President Eisenhower promoted him to the rank of brigadier general stating that Lindbergh's work had significantly shortened the war in the Pacific by enabling pilots to reach many targets formerly beyond their range and thereby saving many lives. In the same year he was awarded the 1953 Pulitzer Prize for his autobiography The Spirit of St. Louis . Billy Wilder directed the movie version starring Jimmy Stewart released in 1957.

Thereafter Lindbergh dedicated himself to conservation causes as an officer and spokesman for the Nature Conservancy, the World Wildlife Fund, and other groups. He announced his growing concerns in a series of articles published in Reader's Digest , one of which included his most famous quote, "I realized that if I had to choose, I would rather have birds than airplanes." In 1966 Lindbergh became a member of the board of trustees of the World Wildlife Fund. His election to this board came after several years of active participation in the conservation movement. Although Lindbergh had been concerned for some time about the pollution of the environment, the encroachment of civilization on the earth's remaining natural areas, and the precarious existence of the world's wildlife, a trip to East Africa in 1964 persuaded him that he should take up the cause of conservation in earnest. Lindbergh traveled extensively throughout the world during these years, to East Africa; Indonesia; Japan; Madagascar; the Pacific Islands and Australia; the Philippines; South America; and throughout the United States. He worked to limit the hunting of the nearly-extinct blue and humpback whales; preserve the monkey-eating eagle of the Philippines; and shield the Tasaday, a stone-age people discovered on Mindanao in 1971, from the assaults of a curious public. He actively lobbied governments and private interests for measures to protect and preserve the natural environment.

He was successful in persuading the Alaska legislature to alter the planned route of the oil pipeline to mitigate its impact on polar bear migration and some countries to limit their whale harvesting. In 1969 he was awarded the Bernard M. Baruch Conservation Prize for 1968. One of his last successful projects was to convince the United States government not to permit America to support supersonic air transportation. For the last thirty years of his life Lindbergh lived in Connecticut, with homes in Switzerland and in Hana, Maui, where he died of lymphoma in 1974. In 1978, his Autobiography of Values was published posthumously.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The papers consist of correspondence; diaries; writings; childhood, school and college materials; financial, legal, and housekeeping records; reports; memoranda; drawings; maps; publications; artifacts; and memorabilia documenting the life and interests of Charles Augustus Lindbergh. The papers form the largest and most extensive collection of his personal, professional, and family papers. They document his work as a pilot, developer of commercial aviation and rocketry, bio-engineer, air force officer and consultant, pioneer environmentalist, Pulitzer Prize-winning author, and public figure. The papers also document his personal life, including his marriage to Anne Morrow Lindbergh, the loss of his son, and his interest in his family history. Notable correspondents include: William Benton, Kingman Brewster, Richard E. Byrd, Alexis Carrel, William E. Castle, Michael Collins, James H. Doolittle, W. L. Glenn, Robert Goddard, Harry Guggenheim, Donald A. Hall, Herbert Hoover, Thomas Lamont, James Newton, Harold Nicolson, Edward Rickenbacker, S. Dillon Ripley, Franklin D. Roosevelt, Igor Sikorsky, Lowell Thomas, Russell Train, Juan Trippe, Billy Wilder, Robert E. Wood, and Orville Wright. Notable family correspondents include his wife, Anne Morrow Lindbergh, and his mother, Evangeline Lodge Land Lindbergh.

The papers are notable for the breadth and depth to which they document the life of Charles Augustus Lindbergh. In addition to containing his correspondence, diaries, writings, and reports that provide a glimpse into how he saw himself and the world, the papers also contain a significant body of material, including publications and unsolicited correspondence, documenting how others responded to his actions and views. His finances and interests are also well documented. The extensive financial, legal, and housekeeping records provide minute details of his and Anne Morrow Lindbergh's finances and households. Memorabilia, maps, and publications collected by Lindbergh provide further evidence of his activities and interests. Despite the size of the collection, it does not represent the entirety of Lindbergh's papers and researchers should be aware of additional collections at Yale and elsewhere. Of primary importance are the related visual materials and supplementary papers in the Lindbergh Picture Collection (MS 325B) and the Anne Morrow Lindbergh Papers (MS 829). Collections of Lindbergh's papers and artifacts, especially those documenting the Spirit of St. Louis aircraft and flights, early airlines, and the kidnapping, are held by the Missouri Historical Society. Aircraft and a collection of aviation-related artifacts are at the National Air and Space Museum. Additional papers relating to his childhood and family home in Little Falls are included in the papers of his father, U. S. Congressman Charles August Lindbergh, at the Minnesota Historical Society.

The collection also includes the personal papers of several family members. The most extensive documentaion regards Evangeline Lodge Land Lindbergh, a science teacher, and Charles Henry Land, a pioneer dentist and inventor of the porcelain crown. Evangeline Lodge Land Lindbergh's (mother) papers include over fifty years of correspondence, financial records, and memorabilia. Charles Henry Land's (grandfather) papers include correspondence, patents, and financial and legal papers documenting his career. A small amount of papers of other family members, such as Charles August Lindbergh (father) and Charles Henry Land, Jr. (uncle), are also present..

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p: The series is divided into two sections: Incoming and Outgoing. In Incoming, all of the letters Lindbergh received after 1926 are filed alphabetically by correspondent; most of the relatively small number of letters received before 1927 are arranged chronologically at the beginning of the section. Incoming letters dated prior to 1927 from a few individuals with whom Lindbergh maintained long relationships are filed with the rest of the alphabetical correspondents. These individuals are: G. J. Brandeweide, James H. Collins, W. H. Conkling, [Ernest G.?] Dixon, Delos E. Dudley, Martin A. Engstrom, Harlan "Bud" Gurney, Albert Bond Lambert, Philip R. Love, H. J. Lynch, Thomas P. Nelson, W. D. O'Connor, Lowell H. Stapf, Albert C. Stewart, and Willard R. Wolfinbarger.

In Outgoing, all letters are arranged chronologically. Lindbergh often penciled in the surnames of his correspondents in the upper left hand corner of his handwritten letters. A check mark next to the name of either an individual or an organization in the address of an outgoing letter indicates how the corresponding incoming letters are filed. For example the incoming letters for:
John Smith ABC Company, Inc. ? New York, NY
would be filed under ABC Company, Inc.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: As a national hero and one of the most widely-recognized men of his time, Lindbergh was subjected throughout his life to a barrage of letters from people all over the world. While many of these letters came from individuals who wished to benefit from the Lindbergh name to promote political causes or business propositions, or from those who merely wished to feel some proximity to a celebrity, a substantial number of the letters Lindbergh received were part of a wide correspondence he developed and maintained over the years following his epic flight.

Select correspondence contains most of Lindbergh's important correspondence with friends, political and scientific associates, and the organizations with which he was affiliated. His correspondents included authors, aviators, businessmen, clergymen, economists, educators, historians, journalists, military men, philanthropists, politicians, publishers, scientists, and statesmen. Of special interest are the carbon copies Lindbergh made of most, if not all, of the letters he wrote between 1928 and 1974. Arranged chronologically in the Outgoing section, these letters form a detailed narrative of the events in Lindbergh's life and illuminate the course of his personal development over the years.

Although most of Lindbergh's correspondence on aeronautical subjects is filed in Series III. Aviation, there are letters in this series that illustrate aspects of his lifelong involvement with aviation. Lindbergh himself kept letters from close friends in the profession, other famous aviators, and various aviation colleagues, separate from his regular aviation files. Among the most important of these letters found in this series are those from Robert Hutchings Goddard and Harry F. Guggenheim. Lindbergh secured the financial support Goddard needed to conduct his pioneering experiments in rocketry through Guggenheim. Goddard's letters to Lindbergh between 1930 and 1940 chronicle the scientist's successes and failures in rich detail. Lindbergh's correspondence with Guggenheim, who was his close personal friend and a trusted advisor, spans nearly half a century and covers a wide variety of topics in addition to the progress of Goddard's work.

Lindbergh the aviator is also reflected in the correspondence he maintained over many years with four other friends: C. B. Allen, Harold McMillan Bixby, Lauren D. "Deac" Lyman, and William B. Robertson. Others with whom he corresponded about aviation include: J. S. Allard, Kenneth J. Boedecker, James H. Doolittle, Sherman M. Fairchild, Earl N. Findley, Henry F. T. Fisher, Donald A. Hall, Clement M. Keys, Thomas G. Lanphier, Hervé Lauwick, William P. MacCracken Jr., Merrill C. Meigs, A. S. Menasco, Harold Nicolson, C. Earl Potts, M. R. Riddick, Vilhjalmur Stefansson, William B. Stout, Eddie Streeter, Guy N. Vaughn, Edward P. Warner, Joseph W. Wecker, Trevor Westbrook, Burdette S. Wright, E. E. Wyman, and Ralph W. Yarborough.

During the 1930s Lindbergh developed an interest in biological research. A chance meeting at the Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research led to a collaboration with the French biologist and Nobel laureate, Alexis Carrel. Under Carrel's direction, Lindbergh invented a perfusion pump in which it was possible to keep tissues and organs alive apart from their organisms. Carrel and Lindbergh published the results of their research in The Culture of Organs in 1938. A man of strong political and philosophical views, Carrel was an important influence on Lindbergh. The extent of this influence is documented in their letters to one another over a ten year period beginning in 1931. Lindbergh pursued other scientific interests that are documented through his correspondence with: Karl Bauer, Richard J. Bing, Joseph H. Burchenal, Lewis L. Coriell, Albert Fischer, Frank Glenn, William W. L. Glenn, Edwin J. Grace, Hayden B. Harris, Archibald Vivian Hill, F. Duran Jorda, Sir Arthur Keith, L. Kervran, W. J. Kolff, Ribert J.S. MacDowell, Theodore I. Malinin, Fred Campbell Meier, John C. Merriam, J. S. Nicholas, Vernon P. Perry, Horace Pettit, William T. Summerlin, C. F. M. Swynnerton, and C. M. Wenyon.

As a resident of England and France during the late 1930s, Lindbergh became increasingly concerned as the general political situation worsened and Europe slid toward war. At the request of Truman Smith, military attaché for Air of the American Embassy in Berlin, Lindbergh made five visits to Germany from July 1936 to January 1939. His visits to German aircraft factories and facilities and evaluation reports are described in his correspondence with Smith.

On his return to the United States in 1939, Lindbergh embarked on a campaign to keep America out of the war. Between 1939 and 1941, he gave numerous anti-intervention speeches (isolationist to his detractors); from April to December 1941, he often spoke under the aegis of the America First Committee. His correspondence on the subject may be found under the names of the following individuals and organizations: Carl William Ackerman, America First Committee, The American Legion, Orland K. Armstrong, William Benton, Chester Bowles, Kingman Brewster Jr., Avery Brundage, Commission on World Peace of the Methodist Church, Hamilton Fish, William J. Grace, Merwin Kimball Hart, Jay C. Hormel, Frederick J. Libby, Ernest Lundeen, Robert R. McCormick, William Starr Myers, No Foreign War Committee, and Paul Seabury. Lindbergh also received thousands of letters from the public in response to his non-intervention stance, which can be found in Series VIII. Letters in response to speeches, 1939-1941.

Particularly important to an understanding of Lindbergh, the public figure and private person, is the correspondence he maintained with a handful of people to whom he felt close enough to express his opinions and feelings openly. In addition to aviator friends previously mentioned, Alexis Carrel, and Harry F. Guggenheim, others include: Amyas Ames, Boris A. Bakhmeteff, William Benton, Henry Breckinridge (who was Lindbergh's legal counsel in the late 1920s and early 1930s), Frederick Coudert, Harry P. Davison, Martin Engstrom, Donald A. Hall, Robert M. Hutchins, Philip R. Love, James B. Newton, Truman Smith, Vilhjalmur Stefansson, Lowell Thomas, William Van Dusen, Helen and Kurt Wolff, and Robert E. Wood. Lindbergh expressed his opinions in a more restrained manner and offered factual information about himself and his family to a number of historians and writers. They include Harry Elmer Barnes, Charles A. Beard, Wayne S. Cole, Francis De Tarr, Bruce L. Larson (regarding Charles August Lindbergh), Milton Lehman (regarding Robert H. Goddard), L. Laslo Schwartz (regarding Charles H. Land), and Alden Whitman.

The series also contains Lindbergh's correspondence with a number of important political, scientific, and literary figures on both the national and international scenes. They include: Spiro T. Agnew, John Foster Dulles, Dwight D. Eisenhower, Albert Einstein, Henry Ford, Barry Goldwater, William Randolph Hearst, Herbert Hoover, Lyndon B. Johnson, John F. Kennedy, Geoffrey Landgon Keynes, John P. Marquand, Jean Monnet, Sir Harold Nicolson, Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis, Philippe Pétain, John D. Rockefeller, Jr., Franklin D. Roosevelt, Vita Sackville-West, and Leo Szilard.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The series consists primarily of letters addressed to Charles or Anne Lindbergh by organizations or individuals with whom they were unacquainted. It includes invitations, fan mail, crank letters, letters in response to their writings, bulletins, newsletters, political pamphlets (especially from right-wing organizations), requests (for autographs, biographical information, employment, financial aid, and photographs; from magazine and book publishers for articles or interviews; and invitations to speak), and letters from inventors (which often include extensive proposals accompanied by drawings and blueprints). Many of the requests and most of the letters from inventors were segregated from the rest of the series by Lindbergh or his staff and are filed at the end of the series. Additional fan and crank mail are filed in Series XIX, Public opinion mail.

processinfo.head: Processing Information
processinfo.p: December 15, 1948 letter from Juliette Lemire (Accession 2022-M-0008) was interfiled into Box 63, Folder 303.

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p: The series is arranged in six sections: Government; Military; Private industry; Organizations; Personal files; and Manuals and navigation aids.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Government is arranged alphabetically by name of agency or branch of government. There is correspondence, minutes, financial reports, annual reports, and technical reports for a number of government agencies, committees, and departments, the most important of which is the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NACA) and its successor, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA). Lindbergh served as a member of and advisor to NACA beginning in 1928 and remained an advisor to NASA in the 1970s.

Military is arranged under the headings, "Army Air Corps," "Army Air Forces," "Air Force," "Missouri National Guard," and "Navy." Correspondence and other materials document Lindbergh's military career, which spanned nearly fifty years, including: his training as a military pilot; his high altitude tests for the Mayo Clinic Aero Medical Unit (1939-1942); his reports to General Vandenberg on the organization, operation, and performance of the Air Force (1948-1949); his participation on the Air Force Academy Site Commission (1954); and his participation on a number of national defense committees (1950s). Correspondence is found at the beginning of each heading and is followed by topical files in order of importance.

Private Industry is arranged alphabetically by company name. Correspondence with a particular company is followed by technical data, organizational, and general files. There are seven files of general correspondence located at the end of the section. Over the years, Lindbergh came into contact with many, if not most, of the people who were responsible for the rapid growth of the aircraft industry, which began in the late 1920s. He developed professional relationships with a number of airlines and aircraft manufacturers. As a result of these relationships, the correspondence, technical data, and other materials in this section provide a wealth of information on the early history of the industry. Of particular interest are the materials relating to Transcontinental Air Transport (TAT), for which Lindbergh worked as a technical advisor from 1928-1930, developing the first transcontinental air route; Transcontinental and Western Air, the successor to TAT, for which he was also a technical advisor and spokesman, particularly during the air mail contracts controversy of 1934; Ford Motor Company and United Aircraft Corporation, for which he worked during World War II developing and testing aircraft; and Pan American, with which he was affiliated from 1928-1974. The extensive correspondence and technical, financial, and public relations/advertising data relating to the development of Pan American is a rich source of information on the history of the company.

Organizations is arranged alphabetically by organization name. It contains correspondence with professional aviation organizations. Personal files is arranged in three sections. Flight logs date from 1922-1944. Private airplanes includes correspondence and other materials relating to the construction and maintenance of three of Lindbergh's own airplanes. Miscellaneous files are mostly comprised of equipment lists and bills. Manuals and Navigation aids contains standard navigation aids used by the Lindberghs from 1930 to 1950.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The materials in this section document Lindbergh's intense commitment to conservation and provide a vivid picture of developments in the international conservation field during the 1960s and early 1970s. Lindbergh's correspondence with conservation leaders and political figures in many countries and with such important organizations as the Citizens Advisory Committee on Environmental Quality, the International Union for Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources, the Nature Conservancy, The Oceanic Foundation, and the World Wildlife Fund illuminates the objectives, successes, and failures of the conservation movement in its political and economic contexts. The accompanying special files materials include publications and administrative records of conservation organizations; descriptive brochures and other publications put out by governments and local interest groups regarding projects in specific geographic areas; and publications about Lindbergh's own involvement in conservation issues.
See also: Index of Correspondents--Conservation.

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p: The series is arranged in two sections: Correspondence and Special files. The material in each section is further divided into three sub-sections: Organizations, Geographic areas, and General. The reader is advised to check both sections to find all materials on a particular subject.

In Correspondence, letters filed under Organizations and Geographic areas are arranged alphabetically. Under General, letters from important correspondents are arranged alphabetically by writer; remaining letters are arranged chronologically.

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p: The series is arranged in eight sections: Books, Articles, Forewords, Speeches, Statements, Diaries, Miscellaneous manuscripts, and Manuscript reference data. Materials in the first six sections are arranged chronologically by date of publication or by approximate date of writing, if unpublished. Materials in the last two sections are arranged alphabetically by subject or type. For related correspondence, see individual publishers and authors in Series I. Select correspondence.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Drafts of Lindbergh's autobiography, which are filed at the end of the Books section, were written between 1938 and 1974. The dates of these drafts often include the words "to" or "closed." These are Lindbergh's notations and refer to the dates on which he placed drafts that he no longer needed in his inactive files. The folder titles are also Lindbergh's.

The series includes working and final drafts of seven books and over one hundred additional publications, as well as originals and typescripts of Lindbergh's personal diaries. In addition to describing his professional and personal interests, Lindbergh's writings reflect his concern to provide an accurate record of his life.

In the years immediately following his flight across the Atlantic, Lindbergh wrote and spoke primarily about his own exploits as an aviator and about developments in the fledgling aviation industry. In 1927 he recounted the details of his flying experiences to Paris in the Spirit of St. Louis in his first book, We . In the 1930s his attention turned from aviation to scientific subjects, and between 1931 and 1939 he published a number of scientific articles and was the co-author, with Alexis Carrel, of The Culture of Organs .

In the late 1930s, as Lindbergh became more interested in world affairs and in political and philosophical matters, he began to work seriously on A Second Letter to Americans , in which he explored the influence of science on Western civilization. Although he worked on this manuscript for several years, he did not complete it. Later, he incorporated parts of it into Of Flight and Life , published in 1948, expanding the scope of his philosophical musings to include a consideration of the importance of spiritual values in a technological society. Between 1939 and 1941, he made a number of speeches in an attempt to persuade Americans that it would be unwise to become involved in the War in Europe.

In November 1937 Lindbergh began to keep a diary of his activities and personal observations in which he made regular entries until 1945. These diaries, edited and cut by approximately one-third, were published in 1970 as The Wartime Journals of Charles A. Lindbergh . Except for the period between 1937 and 1945, he made only sporadic attempts to record his daily activities. In 1938, however, he began to work on an autobiography and family history, a project that would occupy him intermittently for the rest of his life.

Sections of the early drafts of the autobiography were included in Of Flight and Life , and in The Spirit of St. Louis , a re-telling of his flight to Paris, which was published in 1953 and won the Pulitzer Prize for biography. Thereafter, Lindbergh scrapped most of his early drafts and began to work on a new, intensely philosophical version of his autobiography. Assigned various titles over the years, SP , Values , What Man Will Make , Limits , and Form , this work was published posthumously in 1978 as Autobiography of Values .

During the 1950s and early 1960s Lindbergh kept out of the public eye as much as possible and published relatively little. As he became increasingly concerned about environmental problems in the mid-1960s, however, he gave up some of his privacy to speak and write about conservation. In 1972, a series of letters he wrote to the Minnesota Historical Society about his early years on the Lindbergh family farm were published as Boyhood on the Upper Mississippi: A Reminiscent Letter .

The Books section of the series includes drafts and related materials for all of Lindbergh's books, except We . Drafts of his autobiography account for more than half of this section. The letters from readers filed under Of Flight and Life may be of particular interest to historians of aviation. The Articles section contains drafts of twenty-nine pieces dating from 1926 to 1972. There are seventeen Forewords or commentaries on books written between 1930 and 1974 on such subjects as aviation and space flight, exploration, conservation, Robert H. Goddard, Alexis Carrel, and Charles August Lindbergh. Most of the manuscripts in Speeches relate to Lindbergh's anti-interventionist campaign of 1939-1941 or to his conservation advocacy. The Statements section includes his press releases and Congressional testimony on subjects including military appropriations, intervention in the European war, conservation, and supersonic transport.

The Diaries section contains transcripts of his diaries, as well as most of the bound originals. The transcripts were made as a protection against loss and to provide Lindbergh with working copies for his Wartime Diaries project; they include copies of a few originals not found in the section. Lindbergh often wrote drafts of his diary entries and then copied the final versions into the bound volumes; a number of the drafts survive and are filed among the transcripts. The diary entries date from 1913 to 1949.

Miscellaneous Manuscripts contains unidentified drafts and fragments of manuscripts, primarily on the subject of aviation. Manuscript Reference Data includes autobiographical notes, descriptions of scenes and events that Lindbergh wanted to remember, and printed matter.

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p: The series contains materials relating to the families of both Charles and Anne Morrow Lindbergh and to their children and grandchildren. It is divided into three sections: Correspondence, Personal files, and Genealogical records.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Correspondence begins with a chronological run of Lodge/Land family correspondence dating from 1830 to 1929. This is correspondence of Lodge/Land family members who either died before Charles Lindbergh was born or had little or no contact with him during their lives. The rest of the letters in the section are filed alphabetically by author. Charles August Lindbergh's letters, which are addressed primarily to his wife, are important insofar as they reflect on his experiences as a member of Congress and reveal the tension in a strained marital relationship. A small collection of letters (four folders) addressed to the Lindberghs by their children's nurses between 1936 and 1962, is filed at the end of the section.

Personal files contain the papers of family members other than Charles and Anne and include non-family correspondence, private writings (diaries, journals, and notebooks), juvenilia, and in a few cases, professional, legal, and financial papers. The section is arranged alphabetically by family member and the bulk is comprised of the papers of Evangeline Lodge (Land) Lindbergh, Charles's mother. Her papers include correspondence (arranged alphabetically by correspondent), financial records from the early 1920s on, and papers and notes concerning the settlement of her husband's estate. Additional estate files can be found in Charles August Lindbergh's papers, which otherwise have little of note in them. The papers of Edwin Albert Lodge (1822-1887) may be of interest to historians of American science and medicine. Lodge was a prominent homeopathic physician in Detroit and was for many years the editor of the American Homeopathic Observer , a journal of homeopathic medicine and practice. There are two folders containing his notes from medical school, including one of nearly 500 pages on the curriculum medici: physiology, chemistry, anatomy, material medica, botany, theory and practice of medicine, and surgery and obstetrics. There is a twelve page outline (1842) of Gallup's Institutes of Medicine and thirty-one pages of anatomy notes. His diaries and account books document his medical practice. He did lay-lecturing on various topics, including morals, religion, and medicine. There are manuscripts of eight of these lectures (all from 1860), including one on marriage that contains a strong argument in favor of divorce, which is interesting in light of Lodge's own divorce from his first wife, Emma (Kissane) Lodge Rowlands, Lindbergh's great-grandmother. Lodge's reasons for his divorce suit are contained in a 100 page deposition, dated 1855.

Charles Lindbergh's grandfather, Dr. Charles Henry Land, Sr., was a prominent Detroit dentist and developer of porcelain crown technology. His papers include patent records on his inventions, polemical writings in support of porcelain dentistry, and several folders of correspondence with patients (usually satisfied). Harriett (Clubb) Lodge Lindsay's papers include an interesting account of her sea voyage from London to Canada in 1838, including a report of the trip by tow and canal boat from New York City to Buffalo, and a list of expenses and provisions from the trip.

Genealogical records consist primarily of materials collected by Lindbergh. The records are drawn from many sources, and most of them are not documented, especially the typewritten notes on individual family members. The records are filed by family name and include correspondence regarding genealogical subjects; essays and memoirs by family members and others; published accounts regarding family members; and a few legal records, such as marriage licenses and birth and death certificates. The Claims of relationship folders contain letters from persons claiming to be related to the Lindberghs, and the two folders of miscellaneous correspondence are usually with librarians or genealogists concerning branches of the Lindbergh/Morrow families.
NOTE: Evangeline Lodge (Land) Lindbergh wrote parts of her family letters in code. For the key to this code, see her letter to her mother, dated June 16, 1900.

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p: The series is divided into three sections: Financial; Legal, and Housekeeping. Each section begins with correspondence, followed by other materials arranged by type. Four folders containing all of Charles Lindbergh's pre-1927 records precede the correspondence in the Financial section.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The Financial section contains correspondence with banking and investment firms; records of securities transactions; bank statements and cancelled checks; royalty statements; income and property tax records; insurance records; and thousands of bills and receipts for both small and large purchases.

The Legal section includes general correspondence; correspondence and other materials regarding the Lindbergh Cattle Company and the Estate of Charles August Lindbergh; drafts of wills of Anne and Charles Lindbergh; inventories of property and financial holdings; deeds; miscellaneous contracts; and bills of sale for major acquisitions.

The Housekeeping section includes a substantial amount of correspondence regarding various types of purchases, employees, medical care, travel arrangements, schools, summer camps, and the maintenance of Lindbergh houses; appointment and address books; household accounts and inventories; correspondence, financial records, and architectural plans for the Lindberghs' houses in the United States and abroad; and miscellaneous notes and memoranda.

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p: The series is arranged in two sections: Kidnapping and death of Charles Augustus Lindbergh, Jr., and Chronological. The kidnapping mail is organized under topics assigned, presumably, by the Lindbergh's staff. In both sections the materials are grouped by letter or year and month (if known), but a more granular organization was not attempted.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The series consists of mail received by the Lindberghs from people with whom they were not acquainted and to whom they did not respond. The Lindberghs referred to this mail as "C mail." The mail in the series provides a glimpse into the public's response to the Lindberghs from the 1920s until the early 1970s. Of particular note are letters received after Charles's transatlantic flight, after the kidnapping and death of Charles, Jr., and prior to and during World War II.

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p: The series is arranged in twelve groups: A. Family members' writings; B. Genealogies and writings about family members; C. Biographies of Charles A. Lindbergh; D. References to Lindberghs—Aviation; E. References to Lindberghs—Non-intervention in World War II; F. References to Lindberghs—Conservation; G. References to Lindberghs—Scientific research; H. References to Lindberghs—Literature; I. References to Lindberghs—Kidnapping of Charles A. Lindbergh, Jr.; J. References to Lindberghs—Miscellaneous; K. General Work—No specific references to Lindberghs; L. Alexis Carrel's writings.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The Book collection contains approximately 550 monographs, periodicals, and pamphlets relating to the Lindbergh and Morrow families. Within Sections A and L, Family members' writings and Alexis Carrel's writings, works are arranged alphabetically by title. In all other sections of the collection works are arranged alphabetically by author. If more than one edition of a work is present, the editions are arranged chronologically.

This collection should not be regarded as the Lindberghs' personal reading library; it is, instead, a collection of books gathered by the Lindberghs because of the references they contain to themselves and their families. Many of these were sent, unsolicited, to the Lindberghs by authors and publishers and are often inscribed. In addition, the collection contains the writings of family members (Section A) as well as genealogical research on the Cutter, Land, Lodge, Lindbergh, Morrow, and Scott families (Section B), an area of particular interest to Charles Augustus Lindbergh.

The bulk of the collection is works relating to the major interests and events in the lives of Charles A. Lindbergh and Anne Morrow Lindbergh. Biographies of Charles Lindbergh are found in Section C. Approximately half of the works in the collection contain references to the Lindberghs' contributions to aviation, including the 1927 transatlantic flight and later mapping of air routes (Section D). Charles Augustus Lindbergh's evaluations of German and Allied military preparedness and his activities with the America First Committee are contained in Section E.

The Lindberghs' interest in conservation and the protection of indigenous peoples is also documented in the collection (Section F). Charles Lindbergh's early scientific research on aerial mapping, photography of archaeological sites, and the organ perfusion pump is contained in Section G. This section also includes biographical and critical material on Alexis Carrel, Lindbergh's colleague in research on the perfusion pump. Carrel's own writings comprise Section L.

Other sections in the series contain general references to the Lindberghs as authors (Section H), references to the kidnapping of Charles Augustus Lindbergh, Jr., and the trial of Bruno Hauptmann (Section I), and miscellaneous references to the Lindberghs (Section J). There is also a section of general works that does not contain references to the Lindberghs, e.g. Anne Morrow Lindbergh's school books, books given to the Lindberghs by their hosts, and early works on aviation. (Section K).

Numerous works in the series are of interest not only because of their content but also because of the annotations they contain. Charles Augustus Lindbergh was concerned that his career be reported accurately and that credit not be given to him for the accomplishments of less well-known persons; this concern for accuracy is shown in his marginalia. Books so annotated are indicated in the listing of items in the collection.

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p: The accession is arranged in eight sections: Select correspondence; General correspondence; Speech in Philippines; Family correspondence and records; Financial, legal, and housekeeping records; Lindberghs' notes regarding biographical treatments; Writings about Charles Augustus Lindbergh; and Miscellany.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The bulk of the material consists of General correspondence. Much of this material is minor correspondence – autograph requests, fan mail, printed "junk mail," and Christmas cards – from the last years of Charles Augustus Lindbergh's life (1963-1974). There are, however, also many letters responding to his Wartime Journals and to Anne Morrow Lindbergh's Earth Shine , as well as to articles by both. Many of the cards and letters in the General correspondence were never opened by the Lindberghs. They have been grouped together by year, but not by month or day.

Perhaps the most interesting material in the addition are the family members' notes regarding biographical treatments of Charles August Lindbergh that began to appear after his death. The material includes the Lindberghs correspondence with Wayne S. Cole; Anne Morrow Lindbergh's correspondence with John Grierson; and responses from family and friends to Leonard Mosley's biography.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The accession consists of correspondence, writings, and financial and legal records. Much of the correspondence and writings (labeled transcripts) duplicate materials in other parts of the collection. The bulk of the accession consists of financial records that provide minute detail of the Lindberghs' financial accounts.

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p: The accession is arranged in ten sections: Correspondence, Aviation, Writings by Charles Augustus Lindbergh, Writings by others, Genealogical material, Financial, Legal, Housekeeping, Memorabilia, and Miscellaneous.
